strategy:
1. Approach and rationale

Replace population differential evolution and coordinate pattern polling with a convex moment relaxation followed by covariance-guided randomized rounding and single-chain simulated annealing. The relaxation lifts products h[i]h[j] into a symmetric second-moment matrix, so every finite-support lag becomes affine in the lifted variables. A positive-semidefinite constraint and valid product inequalities give a tractable convex semidefinite relaxation for small n. Its first moment and covariance then guide feasible candidate generation. A finite-temperature random walk makes further mass-preserving changes and accepts them according to the exact objective.

This is materially different from the parent and the supplied previous approaches: it uses neither difference-population mutations, an epigraph nonlinear solver, smooth-max gradients, a cosine-coordinate covariance search, exact line-envelope enumeration, nor a quadratic majorization step. The justified facts are that the lifted program contains every feasible rank-one construction, that its objective matches every lag on rank-one points, and that projection and pair transfers can enforce feasibility. The relaxation can provide a lower bound in exact arithmetic, but its solver value is not the returned bound. Recovering a good rank-one candidate from a high-rank solution and improving it by annealing are heuristics. They may improve the parent but are not measured guarantees and do not establish a global optimum. For larger n, skip the dense semidefinite stage and retain the feasible randomized-search path.

2. Mathematical specification

For runtime n, let h=(h[0],...,h[n-1]), dx=2/n, and s=n/2. Feasibility is 0<=h[i]<=1 and sum_i h[i]=s. The authoritative score is the maximum of all 2n-1 scaled finite-support linear-correlation lags. Define
Q0(h)=dx sum_{i=0}^{n-1} h[i](1-h[i]).
For r=1,...,n-1, set m=n-r and define
Qplus_r(h)=dx sum_{i=0}^{m-1} h[i+r](1-h[i]),
Qminus_r(h)=dx sum_{i=0}^{m-1} h[i](1-h[i+r]).
Then C(h)=max(Q0,Qplus_1,Qminus_1,...,Qplus_(n-1),Qminus_(n-1)) equals max(np.correlate(h,1-h,mode='full')*(2/n)). Both directions and each lag's actual partial overlap are essential. Do not wrap indices or replace an overlap sum by a full-mass identity. The exact NumPy expression, not a relaxed objective, ranks and scores returned candidates.

For the SDP, use a first-moment vector v in R^n and a symmetric second-moment matrix W in R^(n by n). A rank-one feasible point is v=h and W=h h^T. Relax the rank-one condition and impose
0<=v<=1, 1^T v=s,
Z=[[1,v^T],[v,W]] positive semidefinite,
0<=W[i,j], W[i,j]<=v[i], W[i,j]<=v[j], W[i,j]>=v[i]+v[j]-1 for every i,j,
W 1=s v.
The elementwise inequalities are the McCormick bounds for products of variables in [0,1]. The last equality is valid because h^T1=s at every rank-one feasible point. These constraints are affine except for the positive-semidefinite constraint and therefore form a convex SDP.

For the lifted lag expressions, use
Q0_rel=dx*(1^T v-tr(W)),
Qplus_rel_r=dx*(sum_{i=0}^{n-r-1} v[i+r]-sum_{i=0}^{n-r-1} W[i,i+r]),
Qminus_rel_r=dx*(sum_{i=0}^{n-r-1} v[i]-sum_{i=0}^{n-r-1} W[i,i+r]).
At W=h h^T these equal the original lag formulas exactly. Introduce scalar t and minimize t subject to every lifted lag being <=t and 0<=t<=1. The upper bound is valid for feasible rank-one points because each unscaled overlap is at most sum(h)=s. Since every original feasible h embeds as a feasible rank-one SDP point, the relaxation's mathematical optimum is no greater than the original optimum. The rank-one constraint was dropped, so an SDP optimizer itself need not represent a useful h; do not return its t as C5.

When a returned SDP point is usable, form its moment covariance Sigma=W-vv^T. The moment constraint implies Sigma is positive semidefinite in exact arithmetic, and W1=s v implies Sigma 1=0. Approximate solver output may violate these identities slightly; symmetrize Sigma, remove its mean-row component to place it in the zero-sum subspace, and clip small negative eigenvalues before using it for Gaussian candidate proposals. Candidates are centered at a feasible projection of v and are projected again after sampling.

For simulated-annealing moves, a direction d must have sum(d)=0. For h+t d, the feasible parameter interval is the intersection over coordinates: if d[i]>0, include [-h[i]/d[i], (1-h[i])/d[i]]; if d[i]<0, include [(1-h[i])/d[i], -h[i]/d[i]]. For a pair direction d=e_i-e_j, this reduces to [max(-h[i],h[j]-1), min(1-h[i],h[j])]. Intersect the interval with the current proposal-radius interval. Every tested point is still projected, checked, and scored exactly.

Joint feasibility restoration is Euclidean projection onto the capped simplex. For a finite proposal z, set P(z)[i]=clip(z[i]-lambda,0,1), where lambda is chosen so sum_i P(z)[i]=s. This follows from the KKT conditions for minimizing one-half the squared distance to z under the box and mass constraints. The sum is monotone in lambda, so bisection followed by a capacity-limited floating-point residual repair implements the projection. Do not clip and then rescale.

3. Implementation procedure

1. Define run(seed=42, **kwargs) and every helper at top level. Use NumPy, math, and optional CVXPY; no closures or lambdas, filesystem I/O, or network I/O. Guard optional imports and solver calls. The generated program performs every search, projection, score evaluation, and fallback decision at runtime.

2. Resolve n, the parent, and the protected fallback. In a guarded lookup, convert the pre-imported initial_h_values to a flattened float64 working vector. If its length is 1 through 999, use that length as n even when kwargs contains n_points. It is a usable parent only if all entries are finite and within [-1e-8,1+1e-8]. Clip only this small accepted tolerance to [0,1], project the parent, and retain that result as the protected fallback and first candidate. If the parent length is valid but its values are invalid or projection fails, retain n and use the uniform vector as fallback. If no valid parent length exists, accept kwargs.get('n_points',47) only if it converts to an integer in 1..999; otherwise use 47. Without a usable parent, use the n-vector filled with 0.5. Parse seed as an integer for numpy.random.default_rng; on failure use 42. Do not redefine, serialize, or hard-code initial_h_values.

3. Implement project_capped(z,n) and is_feasible(h,n). Require a finite vector of exact shape (n,); return failure for invalid inputs. For numerical protection, clamp finite proposal coordinates to [-1e6,1e6] before projection. Set lo=min(z)-1 and hi=max(z). At lo, the clipped sum is n; at hi it is zero. Perform 80 bisection iterations using u=clip(z-mid,0,1), increasing lo when sum(u)>s and decreasing hi otherwise. Form u using the final bracket midpoint. Compute r=s-sum(u). If r>0, visit entries in order and add at most min(r,1-u[i]); if r<0, subtract at most min(-r,u[i]). Recompute the residual and make up to three further capacity-limited passes. Never cross a box bound. Return failure unless all values are finite, all bounds hold exactly, and the absolute mass residual is at most 1e-9. The feasibility predicate checks these same shape, finiteness, exact bounds, and mass requirements.

4. Implement exact_score(h,n). First require is_feasible. Compute float(max(np.correlate(h,1.0-h,mode='full')*(2.0/n))). Return positive infinity on invalid input, exception, or nonfinite output. This exact formula is the only score used for candidate ranking, annealing acceptance, incumbent updates, and the return value. For n==1, return [0.5], its freshly computed exact score, and integer 1 without invoking CVXPY or search.

5. Build a top-level solve_moment_sdp(n) helper for 2<=n<=64; skip it for n>64 to bound dense model and solver costs. If CVXPY import, model construction, or solving fails, return no SDP point and continue with the randomized candidate path. Use variables v with shape (n,), symmetric W with shape (n,n), and scalar t. Construct the moment matrix Z with blocks 1, reshape(v,(1,n)), reshape(v,(n,1)), and W; constrain Z to be positive semidefinite. Add 0<=v<=1, sum(v)=s, W@ones=s*v, and the four elementwise McCormick constraints using the matrices v[:,None], v[None,:], their sum minus one, and zero. Build all 2n-1 lifted lag expressions from Section 2, constrain each to be <=t, constrain 0<=t<=1, and minimize t. Use a scalar loop over r to form each offset sum of W[i,i+r]; do not create a rank-three tensor or a separate Hessian per lag.

6. Only try SDP-capable installed solvers, in order MOSEK then CVXOPT. Do not send this SDP to ECOS, GUROBI, or LP/MIP-only solvers. Use one thread where supported, quiet output, and a finite limit of 200 iterations. For MOSEK use its interior-point feasibility, dual-feasibility, and relative-gap tolerances at 1e-7 and its one-thread parameter. For CVXOPT use max_iters=200 and abstol, reltol, and feastol of 1e-7. Check installed_solvers when available, catch errors per solver, and try the next compatible solver after failure. Accept values only for status optimal or optimal_inaccurate and only if v and W have the expected shapes and finite entries. The solver status and t are not evidence that a returned h improves the exact objective.

7. Form the base candidate pool, always inserting the feasible fallback first. Add algorithmic proposals and send each through project_capped, is_feasible, and exact_score. Deduplicate when max(abs(a-b))<1e-8. Keep at most 192 unique candidates. If a usable parent exists, try its reversal, complement, complement of reversal, and rolls by n//3 and n//2. Also try the uniform vector, a block vector with floor(n/2) initial ones and, for odd n, a 0.5 entry next, an alternating balanced vector, and a seeded balanced random vector. For the alternating vector, set the first floor(n/2) even-indexed positions to one and, for odd n, the next even-indexed position to 0.5. For the random vector, set floor(n/2) randomly selected positions to one and, for odd n, one remaining position to 0.5. Add projected Gaussian perturbations of the fallback with standard deviations 0.05, 0.12, and 0.25, plus eight projected vectors sampled uniformly from [0,1]. Rolls are only start generators; objective scoring remains finite-support linear correlation.

8. If the SDP returns finite v and W, project v to obtain a feasible center and add it to the pool. Form Sigma=W-vv^T, symmetrize it, and project it onto the zero-sum subspace using Sigma <- Sigma-rowmean[:,None]-rowmean[None,:]+grandmean, where rowmean is the vector of row means and grandmean is the matrix mean. Eigendecompose the result. If eigendecomposition fails or inputs are nonfinite, skip covariance sampling but retain the feasible center. If the minimum eigenvalue is below -1e-5*max(1,max(abs(eigenvalues))), treat the covariance as unreliable and skip it; otherwise clip negative eigenvalues to zero and cap positive eigenvalues at n/4. Keep eigenvalues above 1e-10 times the largest positive eigenvalue and form F=V*sqrt(eigenvalues) by column scaling. For each scale gamma in {0.25,0.5,1.0,1.5}, draw 16 seeded standard-normal vectors z, form noise=F@z, and add the projected candidates center+gamma*noise and center-gamma*noise. Every sample is independently projected, feasibility-checked, exact-scored, and deduplicated. If covariance sampling is unavailable, add 24 projected centered-Gaussian perturbations around the fallback with standard deviation 0.15. Update the global incumbent for any feasible candidate whose exact score is at least 1e-12 lower than the current incumbent.

9. Select annealing starts from the scored pool. Always include the fallback first. Then sort the other pool members by exact score and add candidates whose maximum coordinatewise distance from every selected start exceeds 0.03, until reaching the n-dependent cap. If diversity leaves too few starts, fill from the remaining lowest-score candidates. Use at most 5 chains for n<=64, 4 for 65<=n<=128, 3 for 129<=n<=256, 2 for 257<=n<=512, and 1 for 513<=n<=999. The pool itself has already been exact-scored, so a missing or failed SDP does not prevent a valid search.

10. Implement anneal_chain(h0,score0,F,n,steps,rng,best_h,best_score) as a top-level helper. Initialize its current state from the feasible start. Use 600 proposals per chain for n<=64, 300 for 65<=n<=128, 140 for 129<=n<=256, 60 for 257<=n<=512, and 24 for larger n. At proposal k, let rho=k/max(1,steps-1), T0=0.25*dx, Tfinal=0.01*dx, T=T0*(Tfinal/T0)^rho, and delta=0.18*(1-0.75*rho). Use a pair transfer on four out of every five proposals: choose distinct ordered indices i,j uniformly and use d=e_i-e_j. On the fifth proposal, use a collective direction F@z for standard-normal z if a nonempty covariance factor is available; otherwise use a fresh standard-normal n-vector. Center a collective direction by subtracting its mean, set its last component to minus the sum of its other components to reduce mass drift, reject a nonfinite or near-zero direction, and normalize it to max absolute entry one.

For a collective direction, compute the feasible interval by intersecting the coordinate intervals in Section 2, ignoring |d[i]|<=1e-14. For a pair direction use [max(-h[i],h[j]-1),min(1-h[i],h[j])]. Intersect either interval with [-delta,delta]. Skip nonfinite intervals or widths <=1e-12; otherwise draw t uniformly from the intersection, form h+t*d, project it, check feasibility, and skip changes with max(abs(candidate-h))<1e-10. Compute the exact score. Update the shared global incumbent immediately if the candidate improves it by more than 1e-12, whether or not the annealing chain accepts the move. Accept every candidate whose score is no greater than the current score. For an uphill move, accept with probability exp(-(new_score-current_score)/T), implemented as log(max(rng.random(),1e-300)) < -(new_score-current_score)/T to avoid overflow. On acceptance replace the chain's current vector and score. The annealing state may worsen; the separately stored global incumbent may not. Catch invalid directions and per-chain exceptions without discarding the incumbent.

11. After every selected start has been annealed, project a copy of the global incumbent and recompute its exact score. Independently retain and re-score the protected fallback. Choose the incumbent only if its final vector is feasible, its score is finite, and its score is no more than the fallback score plus 1e-12; otherwise choose the fallback. If the fallback fails validation, replace it with the uniform vector and compute that vector's score. Return a copied float64 vector of shape (n,), its freshly computed exact score as a Python float, and n as an integer. Never return t, a lifted lag value, a covariance sample before projection, or a solver-reported objective.

4. Search choices and useful variations

Use the defaults above without preliminary experiments: preserve a valid parent length, otherwise use n_points or 47; cap n at 999; seed 42; use the 80-step capped-simplex bisection, 1e-9 mass tolerance, and 1e-12 strict incumbent-improvement threshold. Run the SDP only through n=64 with MOSEK or CVXOPT, generate 16 Gaussian draws at each of four covariance scales and both signs, and use the stated candidate, chain, and proposal caps. The default annealing temperatures are proportional to dx, with T0=0.25dx and Tfinal=0.01dx; the proposal radius decreases from 0.18 to 0.045.

Reasonable static search variations are an SDP cutoff from 48 to 80, 8-32 Gaussian draws per scale, covariance scales from about 0.2 to 2.0, T0 between 0.15dx and 0.4dx, Tfinal between 0.005dx and 0.03dx, and a proposal radius between 0.12 and 0.25 initially and 0.03 to 0.08 finally. Any result-dependent adaptation must be a fully specified runtime rule; the default uses only geometric cooling and the exact Metropolis acceptance rule. These are heuristics, not correctness conditions. Do not alter the full finite-support objective, both lag directions, the box and mass constraints, joint projection, exact-score acceptance, or protected fallback. No setting guarantees the target score or global optimality.

5. Numerical robustness and memory use

Use float64 throughout. Reject nonfinite parent values, proposals, SDP values, covariance entries, eigenvalues, and scores. Symmetrize covariance before eigendecomposition, tolerate only small negative eigenvalues, and skip unreliable covariance sampling without rejecting a valid projected SDP center. Clamp proposal inputs before bisection, repair mass residual only with available box capacity, and recheck feasibility after every projection. Do not use sequential clipping and rescaling. Catch optional-import, model-building, solver, and individual-chain failures; preserve the incumbent and fallback in every case. The log-domain annealing comparison avoids exponential overflow.

The SDP, its moment matrix, and covariance factor are O(n^2) and are limited to n<=64. At that cutoff the dense matrices are small. For larger n, do not build a dense lifted model or covariance; use the algorithmic starts and tangent-Gaussian annealing moves, which need O(n) working storage apart from the O(n) output of correlation. Each exact np.correlate evaluation takes O(n^2) arithmetic. The fixed proposal budgets bound the number of such evaluations on the one-CPU harness, with progressively smaller budgets as n grows. The candidate pool is capped at 192 vectors. If all optimization paths fail or no candidate improves, return the valid fallback.

6. Runtime safeguards and return contract

The generated program must define run(seed=42, **kwargs) at top level and return exactly (h_values,c5_bound,n_points). It must use a guarded runtime lookup of the pre-imported initial_h_values, never redefine or hard-code it, and perform no filesystem or network I/O. Parent length takes precedence when valid; otherwise validate n_points or use 47. Implement all projections, feasibility checks, objective evaluations, SDP handling, randomized rounding, annealing, candidate acceptance, and fallback selection inside the program.

Before any candidate can update the incumbent or be returned, check its runtime-derived shape, finite entries, exact bounds 0<=h[i]<=1, and mass residual at most 1e-9. Keep the projected usable parent as the protected fallback, or the uniform 0.5 vector when no usable parent exists. Immediately before return, recompute c5_bound from the selected vector with max(np.correlate(h_values,1.0-h_values,mode='full')*(2.0/n_points)) and require it to be finite. If any final candidate check fails, restore and validate the fallback and recompute its score from the same exact formula. Return h_values as float64, c5_bound as a Python float, and n_points as an integer. The coder writes these executable operations only and must not claim to have computed or verified a solution.
